case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J. This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are:

3. Krishnapada Biswas and others, the predecessors of the respondents herein as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.1208 of 1983 against Saburannessa Bibi and others, the predecessors of the appellants, seeking declaration of title in the suit land, which consisted of 30 decimals of land situated in plot No.307 and also 03 decimals of land situated in other plot, both under khatian No.133 of Mouza and P.S. Jhenaidah and also for recovery of khas possession thereof on the averments that above plot No.307 measuring 63 decimals of land belonged to Fazar Ali and others. Subsequently, Sattendra Nath became the owner of the same, and then on 15th Chaitra B.S, 1354, Sattendra Nath leased 30 decimals of land situated on the northern side of plot No.307 to Haripada, his servant, who then constructing a house started living therein. But the survey record was wrongly prepared in the name of Sattendra Nath. On 15th Kartick,1375 B.S, Jagadish disclosed to Haripada that the record of right in respect of the suit land stands in the name of Sattendra and he had purchased the suit land from Sattendra Nath along with other lands. After coming to know about the same, Haripada filed Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 under section 143(a) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for correction of the record of right and then the above miscellaneous case was stayed with a direction to the other side to file a regular title suit by 20.05.1970 and such suit not being filed, decision was given in favour of Haripada on 15.06.1970. During the liberation war, Haripada was shot dead in his own house. From suit plot No.307, which contained 60 decimals of land(but wrongly written 63 decimals in khatian), Jagadish purchased only 33 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath but he in his kabala from Sattendra Nath, fraudulently included the entire land of the plot, which was owned by Haripada and Amanat Mollah. Haripada died leaving his wife Bimala Bala, who sold 03 decimals of land to Manju Rani, respondent No.6 of Civil Revision No.286 of 2001. Then Bimala Bala on 24.7.73 sold 10 decimals and on 01.09.1975 sold 17 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 and Basanti Bala. They dug a pond in 15 decimals of purchased land. Basanti Bala on 14.7.1976 sold 02 decimals of land to Monto Kumar. The defendant earlier filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981, which ended on filing a solenama which was forcefully obtained by the defendants from the plaintiff. Thereafter, defendants forcibly took possession of the suit land on 15.11.1981. Then on 10.10.1982 defendant constructed a straw-hut on the bank of the pond which is situated within the suit land.

4. Defendant (Saburannessa) contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit. Her case, in short, is that Sattendra Nath, the owner of the suit land along with other lands, sold 91 decimals of land to Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 6.9.1963 and also sold 30 decimals of land from the suit land to Amanat Mollah by a registered deed of sale dated 17.4.1964. Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 28.11.1969 sold 91 decimals of land to Saburannessa and she, during the period of liberation war, went to India and then on coming back to Bangladesh, having found her house destroyed, lived in the hospital where she was an employee. In the meantime taking advantage of the death of her husband, Bimala Bala constructed a house on the northern side of the suit land by dispossessing her there-from. The defendant came to know that Haripada fraudulently created dakhila in relation to 33 decimals of land which included 30 decimals of land in the suit plot and also got exparte decree for correction of record in his favour. Then, she filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 for declaration of her title in the suit land and also for recovery of khas possession. The above suit was compromised and a solenama was filed by the parties, on the basis of which, the plaintiff gave possession of only 15 decimals of land to her and took one month time for removal of the house from the suit land in order to handover possession of the balance land but, on 10.05.1982. The plaintiff refused to do so disclosing that in terms of the condition of the solenama, she would get only 15 decimals of land and the rest would go to the plaintiff. Then she, on obtaining the certified copy of the solenama on 25.8.1982, found that the solenama was not correctly written in terms of the agreement made between her and the plaintiff and accordingly, she filed Title Suit No.772 of 1982. The trial Court, upon hearing Title Suit Nos.772 of 1982 dismissed it by the judgment and decree dated 28.04.1991. Against the aforesaid judgment, the defendant filed Title Appeal No.84 of 1992 which was dismissed on 11.06.1994 for want of tadbir, against which the defendant filed Miscellaneous Case No.35 of 1994 which was also dismissed on 02.02.1995.

5. The trial Court, upon consideration of materials on record, decreed Title Suit No.1208 of 1983. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.85 of 1992 and the learned lower appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, respondent Nos.1-6, the successors of Haripada, moved the High Court Division by filing a revisional application and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.286 of 2001. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing both the sides by the judgment and order dated 12.03.2008 made the Rule absolute.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the successor of the plaintiffs as the leave-petitioners have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1767 of 2008 before this Division and obtained leave on 16.08.2009 resulting in Civil Appeal No.288 of 2010.

8. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the appellate Court came to the finding that after lease of 30 decimals of land from suit plot No.307 in favour of Haripada, Satendra Nath had title over 33 decimals of land in the said plot and Krishnapada, the plaintiff in Title Suit No.1208 of 1983 failed to produce any supporting document in respect of the lease made by Sattendra Nath in favour of Haripada and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the appellate Court further held that P.W.2, Lutfor Rahman, the only solitary witness of the plaintiff, son of Amanat Molla, is an interested witness and that the lower appellate Court on proper calculation of the age of P.W.2 came to the finding that the P.W.2 at the time of the alleged settlement was a boy of 9/10 years old and that the High Court Division on the basis of erroneous calculation held that at that time the age of P.W.2 was only 14/15 years and that on that wrong calculation believed his evidence and that Krishnapada totally failed to prove the lease in favour of Haripada by submitting any document and that exhibit-D, on which, Krishnapada relied on is merely the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 which did not create any title in his favour even then the High Court Division made the Rule absolute only on the basis of exhibit-D.

9. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, submits that exhibit-D, the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969, proved that in fact, dakhila was granted to Haripada and that the said dakhila was lost during war of liberation and that the High Court Division erroneously concurred with the finding of the trial Court which held that exhibit-D proved the settlement of Haripada and as such, no interference is called for.

10. We considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment an the materials on record.

11. The trial Court relying on exhibit-D, the certified copy of Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969 and also on the evidence of P.W.2 came to the finding that settlement of Haripada was proved. Haripada filed some dakhilas in the miscellaneous case and that those dakhilas were lost and that the said contention of the plaintiffs could not be disbelieved.

12. The trial Court also came to the finding that Haripada took settlement of 30 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath and that after the death of Krishnapada, his wife Bimala became owner of the said land and that the plaintiff, subsequently, purchased the suit land from Bimala Bala.

13. The appellate Court, on the other hand, came to the finding that the plaintiff claimed that Haripada took settlement of 30+3=33 decimals of land from Sattendra Nath and that on perusal of the record it appeared that no document could be produced to substantiate the claim of settle-ment. The appellate Court also came to the finding that admittedly Haripada was a servant of Sattendra Nath and that it was not believable that Sattendra Nath after settling the suit land to his servant would get the R.S. khatian recorded in his own name in respect of the said land. The appellate Court held that it was believable that subsequently by two deeds of sale, Jagadish and Amanat Molla purchased the entire land of suit plot No.307 measuring 63 decimals of land.

14. The High Court Division, on the other hand, concurred with the finding of the trial Court holding that P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman at the relevant time of settlement was aged about 13/14 years and that P.W.2 stated in his evidence that his father Amanat Molla was serving in serestha of Sattendra Nath as 'Gomasta' when Haripada purchased the suit land from Sattendra Nath and that his father Amanat Molla, wrote dakhila on 15th Chaitra,1354 B.S. and that during cross-examination by the defendant, this witness Lutfor Rahman could not be shaken. Therefore, the High Court Division concurred with the judgment of the trial Court and made the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court.

15. Admittedly, C.S. plot No.307 measuring 1.33 acres of land belonged to Sattendra Nath. The plaintiff claimed that Sattendra Nath settled .30 acre of land from the suit plot to Haripada on 15th Chaitra, 1354 B.S. and subsequently, Haripada constructed his dwelling house on that land and after his death his wife Bimala Bala became the owner of the suit land. The plaintiff also claimed that on 24.07.1973 and 01.09.1975 Bimala Bala transferred .10 acre and .07 acre of land to plaintiff No.1 and Basanti Bala respectively. Bimala Bala also transferred .03 acre of land to Monjo Rani and Basanti Bala transferred .02 acre of land to Monto Kumar Das. The plaintiff also claimed that the defendant filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 and that on the basis of forged sole-nama filed in that suit, the plaintiff on 15.11.1981 entered into the suit land and on 15.10.1982 erected a straw-house on the bank of the tank appertaining to the suit land.

16. On the other hand, the defendant claimed that on 06.09.1963 Sattendra Nath sold the suit land along with .91 acre of land of other plots to Jagadish and also sold .30 acre of land to Amanth Molla. Jagadish by a registered deed of sale dated 28.11.1969 sold the suit land to defendant No.1. Defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No.869 of 1981 which was decreed on compromise. On the basis of the sole-nama, the plaintiff relinquished possession of .15 acre of land and that the plaintiff refused to relinquish the remaining portion of the suit land on 10.05.1982. Subsequently, the defendant obtained certified copy of the solenama and came to know about the forgery. Subsequently, this defendant filed Title Suit No.772 of 1982.

<u>17. The plaintiff claimed that Sattendra Nath settled .33 acre of land to Haripada on 15th Chaitra, 1354 B.S. The plaintiff, however, could not produce any registered deed or dakhila and not even oral evidence to substantiate his claim. P.W.1 in his evidence stated that he did not have any personal knowledge about the alleged settlement. P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman in his evidence stated that when Sattendra Nath settled the suit land to Haripada, his father wrote the dakhila and that his father was the 'Gomasta' of Sattendra Nath and that on the date of his deposition, he was aged at 56/57 years. The appellate Court computed the age of P.W.2 Lutfor Rahman and found that at the time of alleged settlement his age was about 9/10 years. Therefore, the appellate Court discarded his evidence as being a child witness. The plaintiff claimed that Haripada took settlement of .30 acre of land from the suit plot and .03 acre of land from other plot but it appears that the khatian was prepared in the name of Sattendra Nath. It is also admitted that Haripada was admittedly the servant of Sattendra Nath. Therefore, it creates doubt that Sattendra Nath after giving the settlement of the suit land to his servant Haripada would get the suit land recorded in his own name. On the contrary, it appears to be believable that subsequently Sattendra on the basis of two registered kabalas sold the entire land of the disputed plot to Jagadish and Amanath Molla.</u>

18. The learned Assistant Judge relied upon exhibit-D, the certified copy of the Miscellaneous Case No.566 of 1969. But before institution of the aforesaid miscellaneous case, Sattendra Nath sold the entire land of the suit plot to Jagadish and Amanth Molla. Therefore, after relinquishment of the right of Sattendra Nath in respect of the suit land, Haripada filed the miscellaneous case for correction of khatian against Sattendra Nath. The appellate Court, therefore, held that this miscellaneous case was collusive and fraudulent and as such, the decision of the miscellaneous case for correction of khatian was ineffective. It was revealed that the defendants were not parties to the said miscellaneous case and that the defendant disputed the very existence and effectiveness of the said miscellaneous case for correction of khatian. The appellate Court also came to the finding that possession of this defendant is admitted in .15 acre of land out of the suit land measuring .30 acre of land. On the other hand, the plaintiff claimed that he was dispossessed from 05/06 acre of land. Record reveals that the plaintiff purchased the suit land in 1973 and 1975 and prior to that the defendant acquired title thereto. The appellate Court also noted that D.W.2, a child witness, tried to prove the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land but that his evidence was dis-carded by the appellate Court on the ground that at the relevant time he was child witness aged about 9/10 years.

19. In the light of the findings made before, we find substance in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and order delivered by the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court is restored.

20. There is no order as to costs.

End.
